text:
# How Git stores a commit

Every `git commit` you run writes a handful of small files into `.git`. There is no database and no diff log. Git is a key-value store in which the key is a hash of the content, and a commit is a few entries in that store plus one pointer that says where your branch is now.

## The object store

Everything lives under `.git/objects`. Each object is a file whose name is the SHA-1 hash of its contents: 40 hex characters, with the first two used as a directory name and the remaining 38 as the filename. An object with the hash `8ab686ea...` is stored at `.git/objects/8a/b686ea...`.

Before hashing, Git prepends a short header containing the object's type and its size in bytes. It then compresses the result with zlib and writes it to disk. That is why you cannot read these files with `cat`. Use `git cat-file -p <hash>` to print an object, and `git cat-file -t <hash>` to see its type.

Because the name is derived from the content, two consequences follow:

- **Objects are immutable.** Changing a byte changes the hash, which makes it a different object.
- **Identical content is stored once.** The same file in a thousand commits occupies one object.

Three object types make up a commit: blobs, trees and commit objects.

## Blobs: file contents

A blob holds the bytes of one file and nothing else. It has no filename, no permissions and no timestamp. If two files in your repository have identical contents, they share one blob, whatever they are called and wherever they sit.

Blobs are created when you run `git add`, not when you commit. Staging a file writes its blob into the object store and records the hash in the index (`.git/index`), which is the list of paths and blob hashes that will make up the next commit.

## Trees: directories

A tree represents one directory. It is a list of entries, each with a mode, a type, a hash and a name:

```
100644 blob a906cb2a4a904a152e80877d4088654daad0c859    README.md
100755 blob 8f94139338f9404f26296befa88755fc2598c289    build.sh
040000 tree 99f1a6d12cb4b6f19c8655fca46c3ecf317074e0    src
```

The mode records whether an entry is a regular file (`100644`), an executable (`100755`), a symlink (`120000`) or a subdirectory (`040000`). Subdirectories are entries that point at other trees, so the top-level tree describes the whole project recursively.

This is where filenames live, and it is also where Git's efficiency comes from. If a commit changes one file in `src/`, Git writes a new blob for that file, a new tree for `src/` and a new root tree. Every other blob and subtree is referenced by its existing hash and is not written again.

## Commit objects: a snapshot plus context

A commit object is a short piece of text:

```
tree 4b825dc642cb6eb9a060e54bf8d69288fbee4904
parent 1a410efbd13591db07496601ebc7a059dd55cfe9
author Ada Lovelace <ada@example.com> 1762850000 +0000
committer Ada Lovelace <ada@example.com> 1762850000 +0000

Fix off-by-one in pagination
```

It contains:

- **One `tree` line**, the hash of the root tree. This is the complete state of the project at that commit.
- **Zero or more `parent` lines.** The first commit in a repository has none, an ordinary commit has one and a merge has two or more.
- **Author and committer**, each with a timestamp. They differ after operations such as rebase or cherry-pick.
- **The message.**

A commit stores a full snapshot, not a diff. When `git show` or `git log -p` displays a diff, Git computes it on the spot by comparing the commit's tree with its parent's tree.

The commit's hash covers the tree hash and the parent hashes, so it depends on the entire content and the entire history behind it. This is why rebase and `commit --amend` produce new commits with new hashes: they cannot edit the old ones.

## Refs: names for hashes

Nothing so far says what a branch is. A branch is a file containing one commit hash. `main` is the file `.git/refs/heads/main`, and its contents are 40 hex characters and a newline. Tags live in `.git/refs/tags`, and remote-tracking branches in `.git/refs/remotes`.

`.git/HEAD` records what you have checked out. Normally it holds a reference to a branch:

```
ref: refs/heads/main
```

If you check out a commit directly, `HEAD` holds a raw hash instead, which is the "detached HEAD" state.

Creating a branch writes one small file, which is why it is instant. Deleting a branch removes the pointer and leaves the commits in place until garbage collection removes objects that nothing references.

## What `git commit` does

1. Git builds tree objects from the index, one per directory, reusing any that already exist.
2. It writes a commit object that points at the root tree, with the commit `HEAD` currently resolves to as its parent.
3. It overwrites the current branch's ref file with the new commit's hash.

The third step is the only one that modifies an existing file. Everything else is new objects added to the store.

## Packfiles

A long-lived repository will not have one file per object. Git periodically bundles objects into packfiles under `.git/objects/pack`, where similar objects are stored as deltas against each other to save space. Refs can likewise be collected into a single `.git/packed-refs` file. Both are storage optimisations. The model of blobs, trees, commits and refs is unchanged, and `git cat-file` works the same either way.
